title: Royalties, selling tunes outright and not worrying about the business
summary: He got small royalties from "I've Come a Long Ways, Baby", sold tunes to publishers for a flat fee, and just wanted his check.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: I do, sure, but I'm just wondering what kind of -- if you had any second thoughts or -- you know what I mean?
I had second thoughts wondering if I was going to get my money.
How did you feel about all those sessions you did in the '50s where you know, -- I guess in the '30s and '40s there was no question about it. They give you your money and you take a walk.
But in the '50s the whole question of royalties started to come in, of copyrighting.
Royalties come in. I've got a little royalties.
Like, 'I've Come a Long Ways, Baby.' I
And things that I recorded myself. You know, singing and so forth. I got some change for that.
And then I'd have a lot of record dates. By somebody else. They'd take me on the date and I'd wait for my check to come in when it was due, you know.
Naturally. I did the music already and I'd want my money. It wasn't such a hassle, but you know, you wanted to get it over with.
Well, normally, like what kinds of -- when they copyrighted the tune, who copyrighted the tunes that you did, the publisher?
Yeah. Well, I always sold it to them. Understand?
That's what I was getting at. See, my brother has a friend who wrote a tune called, 'At The Hop.'
It was a rock and roll tune.
No, I don't remember that tune.

It was one of those rock singing groups, Danny and the Juniors, you know. Late '50s. Well, I was just thinking, one day in the late '60s this friend of my brother got a check in the mail for $12,000.00.
And it was re-recorded in a best selling album. At Woodstock, they had a big--
That's for sure, you know. But it's not so much luck as business.
Now, of course the people in his publishing company had nothing to do with writing the song, they also got checks like that.
But I was just wondering if like what you felt about the whole business situation in the '50s, as that was changing.
What I thought about it? I didn't worry about it, to tell you the truth.
I didn't worry about it. I just worried about getting my check.
You figured that there was nothing you could do about it personally.
That's right. Didn't understand I could do it if I had to.
I didn't know that. That's the reason why I just went on, you know.
